lead: A test plan names roles and exit criteria. It only happens if real people are staffed, organised and reported on. Testing is done by humans inside an organisation, so someone must decide whether testers sit inside development teams or in a separate group, what each role owns, how new testers are trained, and how results reach the people who decide release. This chapter covers that people-and-reporting side: independence, team structures, roles and skills, the test process, and the reports a test manager writes.
prereq: You need: 5.1 Test planning and test plan components, which fixes roles, schedule and exit criteria.

sections.h3: Independence of testers and the friction it creates

blocks.text: Independence is separation between builders and testers. A developer testing their own code reads the requirement through their design and checks that the code does what they meant, not what the user asked for. Independence buys objectivity; it costs context, because an outsider needs time to learn the system.

items: The author tests their own code: fastest feedback, weakest independence.
Another tester inside the same team: shared context, mild independence.
A separate test group in the same company: its own reporting line, slower feedback.
An outsourced or offshore team: strongest independence on paper, largest context gap.

blocks.text: Friction is structural. A defect report is feedback on a developer’s work, and a tester’s day produces it. Two rules keep it healthy: write every defect about the product, stating what happened and what was expected; agree severity and priority definitions before the cycle. Testers who join requirement reviews prevent defects instead of only finding them (see Unit 2).

Never measure a tester by defects logged. That rewards trivial findings as much as data-loss bugs. Measure coverage of planned cases and defects that escaped to production (see 5.4 Test metrics and measurements).
Four structures are common. Each trades independence against speed and context.

blocks.text: Span of control is the number of people one supervisor can supervise well. For test teams it is usually 1:5 to 1:8; past that, review and mentoring get thin. The figure shows a reporting line of 13 staff: one test manager, a functional test lead with 8 test engineers, and an automation lead with 2 automation engineers, plus a domain expert who consults part-time and sits outside the line.

sections.h3: Roles, skills and growing a testing group

items: Test manager: owns plan, budget, staffing and summary report; escalates risks.
Test lead: schedules cases, reviews test designs, mentors engineers.
Test engineer: designs and runs cases, logs and tracks defects to closure.
Automation engineer: builds the framework and scripts and wires tests into the pipeline (see 5.3 and 5.7).
Performance tester: builds load models, runs benchmarks and profiles results.
Domain expert: knows the banking, insurance or telecom rules; often part-time.

blocks.text: Skills that matter: domain knowledge; test design techniques (see Unit 4, Software Testing Strategies and Techniques); enough SQL and scripting to check data and build small tools; fluency with test and defect tools; writing a defect a stranger can reproduce; curiosity to try the unplanned case; and diplomacy, because every finding is someone’s work.

items: Onboarding: one week on the product, process, defect workflow and test environments.
Domain training: a walkthrough by the domain expert, then supervised testing of one module.
Tool training: test management tool, defect tracker, version control and build pipeline.
Mentoring: a senior tester reviews the newcomer’s first twenty test cases and defect reports.
Certification: an entry-level testing certification (ISTQB Foundation is common) builds shared vocabulary, and does not replace practice.

sections.h3: The test process and the reports it produces

items: Plan: scope, approach, roles, schedule and exit criteria (5.1).
Design: test cases and test data derived from requirements and design.
Execute: run each case and record pass, fail or blocked against the build identifier.
Evaluate exit criteria: compare recorded numbers with the thresholds in the plan.
Report: daily status, weekly progress, and the test summary report at the end.
Closure: archive cases, logs and reports, and record lessons for the next release.

blocks.text: The daily status is short: cases run, passed, failed and blocked, plus the one blocker that needs a decision today. The weekly report adds progress against plan, defect trend by severity, open risks, and what the next week needs from other teams.

The test summary report is the release document. It carries scope and what was deliberately not tested, the build and environment tested, counts of executed, passed, failed and blocked cases, defect totals by severity with open, closed and deferred counts, the escaped-defect rate, each exit criterion with a met or not-met verdict, and a release recommendation.

A single defect report needs an identifier, a one-line title, the build and environment, steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, severity, priority, attachments such as logs and screenshots, the assignee and the status.

examples.question: Write the numbers for the release 2.3 test summary report. During the cycle, 480 test cases were planned. Of these, 456 passed, 18 failed and 6 were blocked. The 18 failures plus 12 exploratory findings produced 30 defects: 12 at severity 1 or 2, 14 at severity 3, and 4 at severity 4. Of the 30, 27 are closed and 3 are deferred (all severity 3 or 4); the product owner accepts the deferral. Two defects escaped to production. The group is 1 test manager, 2 leads, 8 test engineers and 2 automation engineers. Compute pass rate, blocked rate, defect totals, leakage and spans, and recommend.
steps: Severity: 12 at severity 1 or 2, 14 at severity 3, 4 at severity 4; total 30.
Status: 27 closed + 3 deferred = 30; none unclassified, but the 3 deferred defects are still open.
Spans: test manager 1:2 (two leads); functional lead 1:8; automation lead 1:2. The two leads supervise 10 engineers between them, average 1:5.

Exit criteria: pass rate ≥95% met at 95.0%; blocked ≤2% met at 1.25%; no open severity 1 or 2 defect met, because the 3 deferred defects are severity 3 or 4 and the product owner accepted the deferral.
Recommendation: release 2.3; schedule the 3 deferred fixes for 2.4.
examples.answer: Pass rate 95.0% (96.2% of run cases), blocked rate 1.25%, 30 defects, 3 deferred severity 3–4 remain open, leakage 6.25%; spans manager 1:2, functional lead 1:8, automation lead 1:2; release 2.3 with deferred fixes in 2.4.

traps: Believing an independent test group guarantees quality. It buys objectivity; quality still comes from the code, reviews and tests.
Measuring testers by defects logged. This rewards trivial defects and punishes prevention work.
Treating blocked cases as failures or passes. Blocked cases never ran; a pass rate of 456/480 = 95.0% and one of 456/474 = 96.2% measure different things; state the denominator.
Confusing severity with priority. Severity is impact on the product; priority is fixing order. A crash in a rarely used report can be severity 1 and priority 3.
Sending a summary report without the build identifier, so nobody can reproduce the numbers.

quiz.q: Define tester independence and name four levels from weakest to strongest.
quiz.a: Independence is the degree of separation between builders and testers. Levels, weakest to strongest: the author tests their own code; another tester in the same team; a separate test group in the same company; an outsourced or offshore team.

quiz.q: A tester sits inside a development team and reports to the development lead. Nobody interferes. Why is their independence still reduced?
quiz.a: The reporting line decides what counts as good work, so the tester shares the team’s deadline and optimism. They hear the design discussion as the only version of truth and inherit its assumptions. A failure found late reflects on their own lead, which shapes what they report and when.

quiz.q: A plan has 480 cases: 456 passed, 18 failed and 6 blocked. A team reports a pass rate of 456/(480 − 6) = 96.2%. Is the figure valid, and what should the summary report show?
quiz.a: It is valid as the pass rate of run cases: 456/474 = 96.2%. The rate against the whole plan is 456/480 = 95.0%, which counts blocked cases against it. The summary report should show both and name the denominator, because a blocked case hides untested functionality.

quiz.q: Testing found 30 defects and 2 escaped to production. Compute leakage and state what a rising leakage over three releases means.
quiz.a: Leakage = escaped ÷ (found + escaped) = 2 ÷ 32 = 6.25%. A rising trend means tests are missing a class of defect, such as one product area, environment or type of non-functional requirement; change the test design rather than asking testers to work harder.

quiz.q: A test group logs 900 defects in a release, mostly cosmetic, while 12 severe defects escape to production. What is wrong with how the group is measured and managed? Give two changes.
quiz.a: The group is paid for defect volume, so cosmetic findings count as much as severe ones, and prevention earns little. Changes: measure coverage of planned cases, escaped defects and defects found per phase instead of raw counts; add testers to requirement and design reviews, and agree severity definitions with developers so effort goes to severe risks first.

quiz.q: Name five fields a defect report must contain and say what each one prevents.
quiz.a: Build and environment prevent 'not reproducible' arguments. Steps to reproduce prevent a round trip to the tester. Expected and actual results prevent debate about whether it is a defect. Severity and priority prevent mis-ordered fixing. Status and assignee prevent a defect being forgotten. A title and identifier let anyone find and track it.

quiz.q: List the six stages of the test process used for reporting.
quiz.a: Plan, design, execute, evaluate exit criteria, report, closure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is shifting from separate test groups to whole-team testing, with specialists kept for automation, performance and security; this is often called quality engineering. Automation engineers increasingly move into platform and reliability work, because the pipeline that runs tests also deploys the product. Tools now generate candidate test cases and cluster duplicate defect reports, shifting tester value towards risk judgement. Search terms: quality engineering, shift-left testing, test pyramid, defect leakage, exploratory testing.
